extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of science, mathematicians, and scientifically-minded readers interested in foundations and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for forming, defending, and using hypotheses and axioms in mathematical and scientific reasoning — e.g., when simplifying models, what counts as an acceptable hypothesis, and what justifies axioms. Focuses on geometry, axioms, and the relation between experiment and a priori intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confinement to relevant properties in models
rubrics_metrics.description: For scientific convenience we feign objects to be divested of all properties except those which are material to our purpose, and proceed on that plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is convenient to neglect other properties and irregularities when there is no practical necessity to attend to them; but this is a methodological device, not a claim that the object actually lacks those properties. One must restore suppressed properties whenever, and in as far as, their presence or absence would make any material difference in the truth of our conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must relate to real existence and avoid distinct falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis framed for the purpose of scientific inquiry must relate to something which has real existence and must not involve anything which is distinctly false and repugnant to the object's real nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty extends only to slightly exaggerating some properties (assuming an object to be completely what it is very nearly) and suppressing others; hypotheses that clothe an object in false properties are inadmissible. Arbitrary hypotheses about nonentities may be useful intellectual exercises but do not add to our knowledge of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive conclusions are necessary only relative to their suppositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of conclusions (e.g., in geometry) consists only in this, that they correctly follow from the suppositions from which they are deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions of deductive sciences stand to the inductions or assumptions on which the science is founded; these assumptions may be true or untrue but are supposed certain for the purposes of the particular science. 'Necessary' here means necessary given the hypotheses, not metaphysically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include axioms among first principles; some are not definitional hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the first principles of geometry we must admit axioms as well as definitions; some axioms are fundamental truths not capable of being demonstrated and are not merely definitions rephrased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some axioms can be put in definitional form or proved by superposition, there remain two or three fundamental axioms (e.g., 'Two straight lines cannot inclose a space') that are indemonstrable and must be accepted as primitive principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms (certain ones) are true without hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The axioms, both those indemonstrable and those which admit demonstration, differ from definitional principles in that they are true without any mixture of hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some general propositions (e.g., equality transitivity or certain mechanical laws) are exactly true of natural objects and are on a par with mathematical axioms; recognize which first principles are empirical general truths versus approximate hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms are experimental truths — generalizations from observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ground of our belief in axioms is that they are experimental truths; generalizations drawn from observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions such as 'Two straight lines cannot inclose a space' are inductions from the evidence of our senses and receive confirmation in almost every instant of our lives; treat axioms as empirically grounded generalizations rather than purely a priori revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental diagrams can serve as experimental evidence if validated by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Our ideas of form can be painted in the imagination with a distinctness equal to reality; pictures in the mind, if sufficiently accurate, exhibit the properties of realities and may be fit subjects of geometrical experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental contemplation (imaginary looking) can justify geometric knowledge because we have learned by long-continued experience that mental images faithfully represent the properties of real objects; nevertheless this mental 'experiment' rests on prior empirical validation of the image–reality correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivability of the negation does not prove a priori status
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the negation of an axiom is inconceivable does not show that the axiom is known a priori; inconceivableness is often accidental and depends on the past history and habits of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because association and habit make some negations hard to imagine, one should not infer metaphysical necessity from psychological inconceivability. Historical examples show that what was once thought inconceivable later became easy to conceive and true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical certainty from metaphysical necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience can give us very strong conviction of a general truth but cannot by itself establish that a proposition is metaphysically necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although repeated observation may produce belief stronger than for most physical truths, we must recognize that experiential induction, being based on a finite number of observations, cannot logically guarantee necessity across an infinite set of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological origins of conviction must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Our capacity or incapacity to conceive certain alternatives (and thus to feel a proposition necessary) is often due to associative habits of the mind formed by repeated exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a truth is 'necessary' or merely highly confirmed, examine whether inability to imagine the contrary arises from cognitive habit rather than from an intrinsic a priori relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hypothetical/deductive reasoning as instrument, not substitute for empirical content
rubrics_metrics.description: We may deduce consequences from arbitrary hypotheses (imaginary animals or commonwealths) as intellectual exercises, but conclusions from purely arbitrary hypotheses teach what would be properties of nonreal objects and do not constitute additions to our knowledge of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothetical modeling is valuable for illustration and logical exploration; to gain knowledge of nature, hypotheses must be tied to actual objects and corrected when suppressed properties materially affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore suppressed properties when they materially affect truth
rubrics_metrics.description: When we suppress some properties for convenience, we are under the indispensable obligation of restoring them whenever, and in as far as, their presence or absence would make any material difference in the truth of our conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglecting properties is acceptable only as an approximation; failure to reintroduce them when relevant results in error. Example: ignoring thermal expansion is acceptable until it materially alters geometry or magnitude conclusions.
